title: Digital burnout is rising. Are voice calls the path to digital wellbeing?
summary: Digital burnout is rising. Learn how voice calls and intentional communication habits may help reduce screen fatigue.
body_markdown:
In today’s[attention economy](https://www.ooma.com/blog/home-phone/attention-economy-where-your-time-goes/) , every app, platform and inbox is proactively competing for your focus, with smartphones and laptops keeping us reachable 24/7. Between texts, emails and Slack, “talking” to each other often feels less like a meaningful conversation and more like a chore. We may be more connected than ever, but we’re more drained as well.


So what’s actually driving this digital fatigue, and is there a way to communicate that doesn’t leave us depleted? In this blog, we’re looking at why digital communication wears us down, what voice calls offer that text and video don’t and a few habits that can help ease the burnout.


## Why digital communication drains us


Every notification that pulls your attention away from a task may seem like just a minor annoyance, but in reality, they slowly[chip away at your mental bandwidth](https://www.ooma.com/blog/home-phone/psychology-of-simplicity-fewer-notifications-can-reduce-stress/) . Every time you’re interrupted by a notification, your brain has to drop what it’s doing, reorient and then find its way back to focus. That constant context switching is exhausting in a way that’s easy to underestimate.


There’s also the problem of information overload. Microsoft’s[Work Trend Index](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/worklab/work-trend-index/will-ai-fix-work) reports that the influx of data, emails, meetings and notifications has outpaced our ability to process them. The average employee now spends more time communicating (57 percent) than creating (43 percent), and the heaviest users are logging nearly 9 hours a week on email alone and 7.5 hours in meetings.


Even video, which seems like the more “human” channel, has its own cost.[Stanford research on Zoom fatigue](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2021/02/four-causes-zoom-fatigue-solutions) points to the cognitive load of managing your on-screen presence, from exaggerating gestures to seem engaged to being forced to stare at your own face for an extended time. Add in intense close-up eye contact and the loss of natural movement, and it’s no wonder video meetings leave many of us more depleted than a simple conversation should.


Short-form video and social scrolling add even more strain.[Several studies](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.08.27.25334540v2.full) have noted a correlation between heavy short-form video use and “attentional disruption, reduced executive function, emotional dysregulation, and increased anxiety/compulsive use.” As short content trains your brain to expect a hit of dopamine every few minutes (or even seconds), it becomes harder and more draining to sit with slower, more demanding tasks.


Between the digital noise, info overload and screen fatigue, it’s clear our always-on communication tools are asking more of our brains and energy than we tend to realize.


## What voice calls give us that text and video can’t


Even with all the ways digital communication wears us down, voice calls have quietly fallen out of favor. We default to text because it’s quick or video because it feels “necessary” for anything important, and the phone call gets skipped over entirely. But that instinct might be misplaced. Research suggests voice calls are an underrated tool for genuine connections.


[UT Austin researchers](https://news.utexas.edu/2020/09/11/phone-calls-create-stronger-bonds-than-text-based-communications/) found that people consistently underestimate how much a phone call will mean to them. In one experiment, participants reconnected with an old friend either by phone or by email. Beforehand, most assumed a call would feel more awkward and said they’d rather email. But the calls actually went better, with people reporting a stronger bond with their friend over the phone.


A second experiment paired up strangers and had them ask each other personal questions, either by text, video or voice-only audio. Once again, people predicted that texting would feel just as connective as talking, but it didn’t. The people who talked, whether by phone or video, felt significantly more bonded than those who typed. In fact, the voice itself, even without visual cues, seemed to be the key component.


While a text message can convey information, it can also strip out nuance and inflections. Voice carries an emotional layer that turns an info exchange into an actual conversation.


## When a five-minute call beats twenty Slack messages


The same principles can apply to work settings. When a topic is complicated, sensitive or just hard to explain in writing, a call often gets you to a resolution faster and with a lot less friction than a drawn-out thread of messages.


Say you need to walk a teammate through a change of plans on a project. You send a Slack message. They reply twenty minutes later with a question. You clarify. They reply again, still slightly confused, so you send a chain of messages with more context. Twenty messages later and you’ve said what a phone call could have covered in five. Worse, each message adds to the notification fatigue that’s already chipping away at everyone’s focus.


A call skips all of that. It’s interpersonal dialogue in real time, with tone coming through naturally. You can hear hesitation in someone’s voice and address it before it turns into a misunderstanding. The teammate can ask a clarifying question in real time instead of waiting for a reply that might not come through for another hour.


While voice calls are a small shift, the benefits can really add up.[Fewer notifications can reduce stress](https://www.ooma.com/blog/home-phone/psychology-of-simplicity-fewer-notifications-can-reduce-stress/) over the course of a day, and choosing a call for certain conversations can contribute to a sense of genuine social connection with the people you work with.


## Small habits that reduce digital burnout


Calling here and there is a good start, but digital burnout often calls for something bigger. Many people respond by wanting to[break cell phone addiction](https://www.ooma.com/blog/how-to-break-cell-phone-addiction/) altogether, ditching notifications, deleting apps and going phone-free. But the solution isn’t necessarily quitting cold turkey; it’s using digital devices more intentionally. Here are a few habits worth trying:


1. **Call for emotional or complex topics.** If a message involves sensitive feedback, a tough conversation or anything that could be misread in text, pick up the phone. Tone carries context that words alone can lose, and a quick call can prevent a misunderstanding that would’ve taken multiple messages to untangle.
2. **Turn off non-essential notifications.** Muting alerts for things that can wait, like social apps, promotional emails and non-urgent Slack channels, reduces the number of interruptions competing for your focus each day.
3. **Batch your messaging.** Instead of responding to every notification as it comes in, set aside a few dedicated windows to handle texts, emails and chats. It cuts down on the constant context switching that drains your focus throughout the day.
4. **Protect your focus time.** Block out chunks of your day where all notifications are muted and communication waits. Deep work needs uninterrupted stretches and that’s nearly impossible when your attention is being pulled in five directions.
5. **Take more walks.** Steve Jobs was known to take a walk whenever he hit a mental block, and the habit’s benefit seems to be backed by research: a Stanford study found that creative output increased by[an average of 60 percent](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2014/04/walking-vs-sitting-042414) when walking versus sitting. So next time you find yourself stuck, try a brief walk rather than reaching for that phone.
6. **Seek out face time (the real kind, not the app).** If a coworker’s nearby, consider heading over with a quick question instead of defaulting to a message. If you’re working from home, try a coffee shop now and then for a change of scenery and some in-person interaction. It’s a different kind of input than a screen and can leave you more recharged than another scroll break would.


None of these habits require a major change in how you work. It’s just about being a little more deliberate about which tool you reach for and when.


## Could the future of communication be…more human?


Digital communication isn’t going away, nor should it. Texts, emails and chats are still the right call for plenty of everyday interactions. But as more writing gets handed off to AI, authenticity will be harder to come by—and more valuable as a result.


When text can be generated in seconds, a real voice on the other end of the line means something. That’s what makes voice calls worth reconsidering. In a world leaning heavily into automation, picking up the phone, rather than being a step backward, could be a way towards greater digital wellbeing and maintaining human connection in the exchanges that matter.
